The proof bounds |Σλ_{r−i}T_{r−i}(y_j)| by ½C₁⁻¹κ^r ≤ ½|T̃_r(y_j)|, which gives exactly this signed ratio. Item 32 records '|T(y_i)/T̃_r(y_i)| ≥ 1/2'. The proof of Lemma 4.7 on p.26 needs the sign. Its claims 'By Lemmas 4.4 and 4.5, this set has cardinality r' and 'T(y_i) and T(y_{i+1}) have opposite signs' hold only because T has the sign of T̃_r at every y_i. That makes T change sign on the r intervals where T̃_r does. With the absolute value, T could keep one sign across such an interval, and S would not be determined. Item 54 says 'for the real ones this places the conjugates in [−2√q, 2√q]', and item 43's note says the same. A real Weil q-number has |π| = √q, so it is ±√q. The number whose conjugates lie in [−2√q, 2√q] is x = π + q/π = π + π̄, a totally real algebraic integer. #A(F_q) = ∏(1 − π_i) = ∏(q + 1 − x_j), which is why Proposition 5.12 uses F(x) = log|q + 1 − x|. This matches the paper's remark on p.4 that 'the study of Weil numbers reduces to the study of totally real algebraic integers whose conjugates lie in certain intervals'. The proposed fixes are right. Severity: Low is right for items 54 and 43. The item 32 part is closer to medium. Its weakened statement is true, but it does not support its only consumer, item 34 (Lemma 4.7), which uses the sign, so a node built from item 32 as written would have to be restated. It is a one-symbol change in the file that finding 1's fix edits anyway.

I checked all four in the TeX and on page images. All are real, none is among E1–E7, and none changes a stated result. (a) p.24: T̃_r keeps only roots in Σ, so the quotient T_{r+3k₀}/T̃_r carries every root outside Σ, and the same proof allows up to k₀ − 1 of them. For symmetric Σ, uniqueness in Lemma 4.2 gives T_n(−x) = (−1)^n T_n(x). So an odd-degree T_{r+6} vanishes at 0 ∉ Σ. The bound survives: alternation puts a root in each (x_i, x_{i+1}), all r+3k₀ of them, so the roots lie in [min Σ, max Σ]. The degree-3k₀ quotient is then at most (max Σ − min Σ)^{3k₀} on Σ. (b) p.27: there are D+1 points v_{i,0}, …, v_{i,D}. The uniqueness count needs Dr intervals, and the proof later says '0 ≤ j < D', so '[0, D−1)' is a misprint. (c) p.16: P_k is defined for 1 ≤ k ≤ n+1, and the next display takes the max over k ≤ n+1. Lemma 2.8 applies to every k. (d) p.27: at k = 0 the claim contradicts (4.8), which Q satisfies by construction. With 1 ≤ k ≤ N/a, the pigeonhole gives only ⌊N/a⌋ ≤ n, that is N < (n+1)a. Yet (4.9) holds: by minimality [0, N) lies in the union of at most n open intervals of shifts that violate (4.8), each of length at most a. Corrected fix: Apply the fix with two corrections. (1) The example in (a) breaks the standing hypothesis of §4.2 that κ > 1. [−2,−1] ∪ [1,2] is the preimage of [1,4] under x ↦ x², so its capacity is (3/4)^{1/2} ≈ 0.87. Use Σ = [−3,−1] ∪ [1,3] instead: it has capacity √2 > 1 and k₀ = 2, and the argument is unchanged. (2) In (d), write 'open intervals of length at most a': for a nonreal root α the interval {N′ : |Q′(α) + N′| < a/2} is shorter than a. A simpler correct text also works: 'for all k with 0 ≤ k < N/a, some α has |(Q − N + ka)(α)| < n⁻¹C₂⁻¹κ^{Dr}', and then the pigeonhole gives ⌈N/a⌉ ≤ n. Lead check: for Σ = [−b, −a] ∪ [a, b] the map z ↦ z² gives cap(Σ) = √((b² − a²)/4), so [−2,−1] ∪ [1,2] has capacity √3/2 < 1 and [−3,−1] ∪ [1,3] has capacity √2, as stated.
